media_work.title: Convicting the Innocent: Where Criminal Prosecutions Go Wrong
media_work.focus_or_theme: Systematic analysis of DNA exonerations, patterns in wrongful convictions
media_work.key_statistics: Examines the first 250 DNA exonerations in the United States

key_quotes_raw: "In this unsettling in-depth analysis, Brandon Garrett examines what went wrong in the cases of the first 250 wrongfully convicted people to be exonerated by DNA testing."
"DNA exonerations have shattered confidence in the criminal justice system by exposing how often we have convicted the innocent and let the guilty walk free."
systemic_issues_raw: Coercive interrogation techniques leading to false confessions
policy_recommendations_raw: Improved forensic science standards and oversight
Expanded access to post-conviction DNA testing
additional_resources_raw: DNA Exonerations Database maintained by the author
Follow-up academic papers by Brandon Garrett, including "Convicting the Innocent Redux"

research_notes_other.this_book_is_particularly_valuable_for_o:
1. Provides a comprehensive academic analysis of a large sample of DNA exonerations
2. Identifies patterns and systemic issues across multiple cases rather than focusing on individual stories
3. Is written by a leading legal scholar in the field of wrongful convictions (Brandon L. Garrett, L. Neil Williams, Jr. Professor of Law at Duke University School of Law)
4. Uses empirical data and trial records to document exactly what went wrong in each case
5. Offers evidence-based policy recommendations for preventing wrongful convictions
6. Has been influential in shaping legal scholarship and policy discussions around wrongful convictions
The book stands out from others in our research as it takes a more academic, data-driven approach to analyzing wrongful convictions rather than focusing primarily on personal narratives. It examines the systemic patterns across hundreds of cases, providing a broader perspective on the factors that contribute to wrongful convictions in the American criminal justice system.

media_item.item_title: Book Content: Convicting the Innocent: Where Criminal Prosecutions Go Wrong
media_item.focus_or_theme: Systematic analysis of DNA exonerations, patterns in wrongful convictions
media_item.summary_notes: This book systematically analyzes the first 250 DNA exonerations in the US, identifying patterns and systemic issues contributing to wrongful convictions.  It uses empirical data and trial records to document the failures in each case, offering evidence-based policy recommendations for prevention.
media_item.case_details_raw: Multiple individuals (250 DNA exonerees) across various locations in the United States were wrongfully convicted of primarily serious violent crimes (murder, rape).  Their convictions spanned various years, and their exonerations occurred prior to 2011. Sentences varied, including death sentences, and time served also varied.

featured_individuals.case_location: Various locations across the United States
featured_individuals.cross_reference: Book 4: "Actual Innocence" by Jim Dwyer, Peter Neufeld & Barry Scheck
